passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday. Observed at the athletics ground, 4 p.m.
Coach asked Keerthana (15, squad captain) to run a punishment set for Sahil, who had missed Monday's practice. First it was 'two laps, just to remind him.' Keerthana blew the whistle and held the stopwatch. After the second lap Sahil was bent over, and she looked at Coach. Coach said calmly, 'Continue. It's for his own good.' Keerthana's hands were shaking on the stopwatch. She said 'one more' four more times, each time quieter, glancing back at Coach instead of at Sahil.
At that point I walked over, stopped the set and sat Sahil in the shade with water. Keerthana burst into tears: 'I didn't know how to stop once I'd started.' I spoke with her afterwards and raised the punishment laps with the head of sports the same afternoon.

qa.q: How many laps was the punishment set at first?
qa.a: At first it was 'two laps, just to remind him.'

qa.q: What does Keerthana glancing back at Coach instead of at Sahil suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Keerthana was full of doubt and leaning on Coach's calm to carry the responsibility, rather than facing Sahil's distress.

qa.q: Where was the easiest point for Keerthana to stop, and why?
qa.a: After the second lap, when Sahil was bent over; as Keerthana said, it got harder to stop once each 'one more' had piled up.

qa.q: How might Sahil have experienced his own captain calling 'one more'?
qa.a: Sahil might feel let down by his captain, while also noticing her voice growing quieter, as if she didn't want to do it.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenage captain continuing a coach's calm punishment set step by step while visibly distressed.

passage:
Sunday night. I feel sick. Lakshmi-di is directing the annual play and I'm her assistant, so on Wednesday when she said, 'Move Rupa to the back row, she's too short for the front,' I did it. Easy. Thursday: 'Give Rupa's two lines to Anu.' I did that too, even though Rupa had practised them in the corridor all week. Today di said, calm as anything, 'Just tell her she's out. You've done the hard part already.' And somehow that was true: saying no now felt like saying the last four days were wrong. So I told Rupa. My voice shook the whole time and afterwards I went to the washroom and cried. Why was stopping harder than carrying on?
— Bidisha

qa.q: What did Lakshmi-di ask on Thursday?
qa.a: 'Give Rupa's two lines to Anu.'

qa.q: Why did saying no feel so hard for Bidisha by Sunday?
qa.a: Bidisha felt trapped: refusing now would mean the last four days were wrong, so carrying on seemed easier than stopping.

qa.q: Which day would have been the best point for Bidisha to push back, and how?
qa.a: Wednesday, at the first small step: Bidisha could have calmly asked why height mattered and suggested keeping Rupa in the front row.

qa.q: How might Rupa see these four days?
qa.a: Rupa, who practised her lines in the corridor all week, would likely feel pushed out bit by bit and hurt that it came through Bidisha 😢

grounding: A teenager's diary shows a senior's calm, step-by-step instructions leading them to cut a junior from a play while distressed.

passage: The scout camp was held in the school ground of a kasba outside Satara. Ganga, fifteen, was patrol leader, and the senior troop leader, Farhan, was a college boy everyone admired. When little Sonu came to assembly without his scarf, Farhan said calmly, "Ganga, make him stand in the sun. Just five minutes." Ganga did. Five minutes later: "Now arms out. Just continue." She hesitated. Sonu's lips were dry. "It's discipline. Continue," Farhan said, without raising his voice. Ganga's throat was tight, and her voice shook as she said, "Arms up, Sonu." Stopping now felt like saying the first five minutes were wrong. Then the scout teacher, Mrs Pillai, crossed the ground, stopped it at once, sat Sonu in the shade with water, and spoke to Farhan and Ganga separately before lunch.

qa.q: What did Sonu forget to bring to assembly?
qa.a: He came without his scarf.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she kept giving the orders?
qa.a: She felt tense and doubtful, her throat tight and her voice shaking, yet stopping felt harder because it would mean the first step had been wrong.

qa.q: At what point could Ganga have stopped, and how?
qa.a: At the first order she could have said calmly that making Sonu stand in the sun was not right, before each small step made stopping harder.

qa.q: How did it feel for Sonu to be punished through Ganga?
qa.a: Sonu was left thirsty and exposed in the sun, made to obey an older scout, with no one stepping in until the teacher came.

grounding: A teenager told by an admired senior to punish a junior complies step by step while visibly distressed, because stopping feels harder than going on.

passage: The school newspaper office in Accra smelled of printer ink. Yara, sixteen, had just joined as a junior editor, and Nkechi, the senior editor, was someone she wanted to impress. "Review Kwesi's poem for Friday's issue," Nkechi said calmly. "Be honest. Start with the rhymes." Yara wrote that the rhymes were weak. Nkechi read over her shoulder. "Good. Now add a line about how it sounds like a birthday card." Yara typed it. Her stomach clenched. "And say readers deserve better. Just continue, you're doing fine." Yara's fingers hovered. Kwesi was in Form 2 and had shown her the poem in the corridor, shyly. But she had already written two lines; deleting them now felt like admitting she'd been wrong from the start. She typed the third sentence with her face burning, and felt, strangely, like she was watching someone else do it.

qa.q: What did Nkechi tell Yara to start with in the review?
qa.a: Nkechi told Yara to start with the rhymes.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling when her fingers hovered over the keyboard?
qa.a: She was torn and distressed, knowing Kwesi had shyly shown her the poem, but deleting the first lines felt like admitting she had been wrong.

qa.q: What could Yara still do before Friday's issue goes out?
qa.a: She could tell Nkechi she is not comfortable publishing a mocking review and rewrite it as fair, kind feedback, since the review is not printed yet.

qa.q: How might Kwesi feel if the review is published as it is?
qa.a: Kwesi would probably feel humiliated in front of the school, especially after trusting Yara enough to show the poem in the corridor.

grounding: A teenager guided calmly by a senior writes a harsher and harsher review of a junior's poem, distressed but finding it harder to stop than to continue.
